deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous folio, items 1–6). For a prime p with 2^p−1 prime, Ramanujan calls the exponent p a 'Mersenne's prime'. His conjecture (1) is that every such p has the form a^2+ab+b^2 or a^2+b^2. Hence (2): p is never ≡ 11 (mod 12).

He splits the exponents into two classes.
- Class 1: p = a^2+ab+b^2, i.e. p = 3 or p ≡ 1 (mod 6). His list: 1, 3, 7, 13, 19, 31, 61, 127.
- Class 2: sums of two squares not of that form, i.e. p = 2 or p ≡ 5 (mod 12). His list: 2, 5, 17, 89, 257.

Theorem (4) says that if P is prime, p is an odd prime, and (P^p−1)/(P−1) or (P^p−1)/(p(P−1)) is prime, then that prime is a class-1 exponent.
- Case p=3 is (5): if P^2+P+1 or (P^2+P+1)/3 is prime, it is a class-1 exponent.
- Case P=2 is (6): if p is an exponent, then 2^p−1 is a class-1 exponent. This is a Catalan-type double-Mersenne claim.

This folio.

Examples of (5):
- 1^2+1+1 = 3 (P=1 used, though 1 is not prime).
- 2^2+2+1 = 7.
- 3^2+3+1 = 13.
- 5^2+5+1 = 31.
- (7^2+7+1)/3 = 57/3 = 19.
- 11^2+11+1 = 133 = 7·19 is composite and not divisible by 3, so P=11 gives nothing.
- (13^2+13+1)/3 = 183/3 = 61.
- 17^2+17+1 = 307, which is prime, so the claim is that 2^307−1 is prime.
- (19^2+19+1)/3 = 381/3 = 127.
Conclusion: 2^p−1 is claimed prime for p = 3, 7, 13, 31, 19, 61, 307, 127.

Examples of (6):
- 2^2−1 = 3, hence 2^3−1 = 7 is prime.
- Hence 2^7−1 = 127 is prime.
- Hence 2^127−1 is prime; the implied next step would be 2^(2^127−1)−1.
- 2^5−1 = 31, hence 2^31−1 is prime; the implied next step would be 2^(2^31−1)−1.

(7) From the residue classes in (3), the number of class-2 exponents should be about half the number of class-1 exponents.
- [My gloss] Among primes, p ≡ 1 (mod 3) has density 1/2 and p ≡ 5 (mod 12) has density 1/4. Excluding 11 (mod 12) by (2) gives the ratio 1/2.

(8) The analogue of (6) for class 2: if 2^p+1 is prime, then 2^p+1 is a class-2 exponent, i.e. 2^(2^p+1)−1 is prime. Examples:
- 3 gives 2^3−1.
- 5 gives 2^5−1.
- 17 gives 2^17−1.
- 257 gives 2^257−1.
Since 2^p+1 prime forces p to be a power of 2, this says that 2^F−1 is prime for every Fermat prime F.

(9) Every class-2 exponent has the form (2^a)^2+(4b+1)^2, with 0 ≤ 4b+1 ≤ 2^a. For every a ≥ 0 there is at least one admissible b.
- a=0: 1+1 = 2, giving 2^2−1.
- a=1: 4+1 = 5, giving 2^5−1.
- a=2: 16+1 = 17, giving 2^17−1 (b=0 forced, since 5 > 4).
- a=3: b ∈ {0,1}. 64+1 = 65 = 5·13 is composite, so b=1 and 64+25 = 89 is prime, giving 2^89−1.
This implicitly asserts infinitely many Mersenne primes, at least one class-2 exponent per a.

(10) Another analogue of (8): if 2^p+1 is prime, then 2^(2^p)+1 is prime. The intended examples are deleted ('Hence we have' is struck through).
- [Mine] The chain would run 3→5, 5→17, 17→65537, 257→F_8 = 2^256+1.

The overall purpose is a speculative structure theory of Mersenne exponents: residue restrictions, generating recurrences from cyclotomic values, Fermat-type chains, and a parametrisation of class 2. Hardy's own heading on the previous folio reads 'purely conjectural'.
errors: (1)/(2) are false: 107 ≡ 11 (mod 12) and 2^107−1 is prime (Powers, 1914). Other Mersenne exponents ≡ 11 (mod 12) exist, e.g. 86243.
(5) applied to P=17 asserts 2^307−1 is prime; it is composite (proved by Lucas–Lehmer testing in the 20th century).
(5) is used with P=1, which is not prime.

(6) is false in general. p=13 gives 2^8191−1, which is composite (Wheeler, 1953). The double Mersennes M_{M_17}, M_{M_19} and M_{M_31} also have known factors. The example 2^31−1 is itself correctly prime, but (6) implies M_{M_31} is prime, which is false.
(8) fails at 257: 2^257−1 is composite (Kraitchik 1922; Lehmer 1927). It also fails at 65537, since 2^65537−1 is composite.
(8)'s first example (3 → 2^3−1) uses 3, which Ramanujan himself placed in class 1 in (3), so it is not a class-2 example.
(9) fails. For a=4 no admissible value works: 257, 281, 337 and 425 are each composite or a non-Mersenne exponent. So 'at least one b for every a' is false.
(9) is also contradicted by the class-2 exponent 521 (≡ 5 mod 12). Its only representation as a sum of two squares is 20^2+11^2, which is not of the form 4^a+(4b+1)^2.
(10) is false: 2^256+1 = F_8 is composite (Morehead & Western, 1909, already known when this was written), and F_16 is also composite.
(7) is a heuristic density claim, not derivable from (3); the true asymptotic distribution of Mersenne exponents mod 12 is unknown.
General logical gap: (1) is a mere conjecture, and the 'inference' to (2) rests entirely on it.

results.what: Mersenne exponents are never ≡ 11 (mod 12), i.e. are of the form a^2+ab+b^2 or a^2+b^2
results.modern_name: false conjecture on Mersenne exponents mod 12 (counterexample p=107)
results.usually_credited_to: not standard; refuted by Powers' 1914 proof that M_107 is prime

results.what: If p is a Mersenne exponent, then 2^p−1 is also one (double Mersenne chain 2→3→7→127→M_127)
Cyclotomic values P^2+P+1 or (P^2+P+1)/3, when prime, are Mersenne exponents
results.modern_name: false heuristic conjecture (fails at P=17, giving 307)

results.what: If F = 2^p+1 is a Fermat prime, then 2^F−1 is prime
results.modern_name: related to the New Mersenne Conjecture's Fermat-number condition; false (fails at 257)
results.usually_credited_to: Mersenne's list (1644); New Mersenne Conjecture by Bateman–Selfridge–Wagstaff (1989)

results.what: Class-2 Mersenne exponents are of the form 4^a+(4b+1)^2 with 4b+1 ≤ 2^a, at least one for each a
results.modern_name: false parametrisation conjecture (fails at a=4; counterexample 521)

results.what: If 2^p+1 is prime then 2^(2^p)+1 is prime

deep.surprise_reason: These are early, explicitly conjectural and mostly false speculations on Mersenne and Fermat primes, echoing Mersenne's 1644 list (which included 257 and omitted 61, 89 and 107) and Catalan's double-Mersenne chain. Several were already refuted or refutable at the time (e.g. F_8 composite, 1909). The page is of biographical interest only; there is no hidden correct result.
